verdict.reasoning: Patient describes new swelling of the upper lip after eating prawn soup: 'there is like a swelling on my upper lip and it's kind of getting bigger' and this followed 'I ordered a prawn soup'.

'How long did it take to develop the swelling?' / 'must have been like, I don't know, half an hour maybe' after having the prawn soup, indicating onset about 30 minutes after ingestion, affecting the upper lip.

Patient reports breathing difficulty and possible chest tightness: 'I feel like I can't breathe that well' and 'Chest just generally feels a little difficult... it might be. I'm not sure.' This supports dyspnea with possible chest tightness.

She ate the soup 'maybe like around seven' and swelling developed in 'half an hour maybe' and is 'kind of getting bigger. It feels like it's getting worse.' This supports ingestion at ~1900, swelling ~1930, and ongoing worsening.

Transcript: 'I woke up the next morning quite swollen up and... quite difficult breathing' after a late-night Chinese curry. There is no statement that this self-resolved with salbutamol; salbutamol is described as her usual asthma medication, not specifically used for that episode.
Patient explicitly states: 'I generally have asthma, so I... take... Salbutamol inhalus... I've always taken it. I generally have asthma.'

Transcript confirms peanut allergy and a childhood hospital visit with an injection: 'I have a peanut allergy as well' and 'my mom ever said that you had to go to hospital because you had a severe allergic reaction? ... yeah, well, I was like six or something.' However it does not explicitly state this was anaphylaxis or specify 'emergency department' wording; that is an inferred label and location not in the transcript.

Patient: 'I generally have asthma, so I... take... Salbutamol inhalus... I do take that regularly.' This supports use of a salbutamol inhaler; frequency ('as needed') is not specified but using salbutamol is correct.
Patient: 'And so do you use antihistamines...?' / 'Sometimes, but I don't know which ones.' This supports occasional use of unspecified antihistamines.
Patient clearly states: 'So I have a peanut allergy as well. Yeah, like always had it?'
While a reaction followed prawn soup (possible shellfish trigger), the transcript never labels this as 'possible shellfish allergy'; that interpretation is not explicitly discussed.

Doctor: 'it sounds like you could be going into what we say, anaphylactic reaction. That's when your throat and your chest closes in and you might need an injection.' Patient has lip swelling and breathing difficulty. This supports suspected anaphylaxis with oropharyngeal angioedema and respiratory compromise due to the prawn soup (a shellfish).
Asthma as baseline is stated ('I generally have asthma') and only salbutamol is used: 'do you use any other inhalers?... No, I don't think so.' This supports asthma managed with salbutamol only.

Doctor: 'I think we need to call an ambulance... I'll call the ambulance. Okay. And I'll send them right to you.' and later asks mom 'if you can call the 999... they need to come straight away.' This matches immediate 999/EMS transport to hospital.

Doctor: 'Could you ask the person whether they have any antihistamines around in the interim while we are waiting?' and 'So straight away, take the antihistamines in the meantime.' This supports on-site oral antihistamine while awaiting EMS.
The transcript mentions only that she 'might need an injection' and to go to hospital; it does not specify intramuscular adrenaline, airway monitoring, steroids, or nebulised bronchodilator.

Post-discharge plan in transcript is limited to: 'Do give us a ring back. We might need to sort you out with your injections and things like that.' There is no specific mention of prescribing two EpiPens, arranging an allergy clinic, or testing for shellfish/peanut with an action plan.
The doctor does not discuss reinforcing salbutamol use or adding a preventer inhaler at GP review; this future asthma management step is not mentioned.
